entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Palace of Versailles, located just outside Paris, France, was commissioned in 1661 by King Louis XIV, who sought to consolidate his power and showcase the grandeur of the French monarchy. The palace became a symbol of the absolute monarchy of the Ancien Régime and epitomized the artistic and architectural achievements of the French Baroque style. As the royal residence, it played a central role in the politics of France and, by extension, Europe during the 17th and 18th centuries.

Construction of the Palace of Versailles transformed a modest hunting lodge into a sprawling complex featuring the Hall of Mirrors, extensive gardens designed by André Le Nôtre, and numerous opulent rooms. This transformation was part of Louis XIV's broader strategy to centralize power by moving the court from Paris to Versailles in 1682, effectively creating a stage for the performance of royal authority. The court at Versailles became a center for political maneuvering and social life, influencing European court culture and diplomacy.

The legacy of Versailles extends beyond its architectural grandeur; it became a model for royal palaces across Europe and influenced the design of numerous gardens and estates. The Treaty of Versailles in 1919, which marked the end of World War I, also linked the palace's history to significant global events. Today, the Palace of Versailles is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, attracting millions of visitors each year, standing as a testament to the power dynamics of its time.

As Louis XIV proclaimed, 'L'État, c'est moi' (I am the state), the Palace of Versailles encapsulates the essence of monarchical power in the early modern period and serves as a reminder of the extraordinary lengths to which rulers went to manifest their authority.
